title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulation Environments
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates powerful self-evolving reasoning for code and math, it remains confined to symbolic domains with deterministic verifiers. Physical and spatial reasoning—critical for robotics and embodied AI—requires understanding causal, geometric, and temporal relationships that symbolic executors cannot verify. Can the Absolute Zero paradigm extend to embodied domains where a simulation environment serves as the verifiable reward oracle?

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, where a language model simultaneously proposes and solves spatial/physical reasoning tasks grounded in a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or Isaac Gym). The model generates task descriptions (scene configurations, causal questions, trajectory planning puzzles), executes them in simulation to obtain ground-truth outcomes, and trains via RLVR using simulation outcomes as verifiable rewards. A task difficulty estimator filters proposals to maintain curriculum progression, analogous to AZR's dequeue mechanism but adapted for continuous state spaces.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark against supervised baselines on SpatialBench, CLEVR, and PhysicalIQA; (2) Ablate simulation-as-verifier versus symbolic verifier; (3) Evaluate zero-shot transfer to real robot manipulation tasks; (4) Measure curriculum evolution—whether proposed tasks exhibit increasing physical complexity over training; (5) Compare scaling behavior across 7B/14B/70B models.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Evolving Curricula with Visual Code Execution
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates impressive self-supervised reasoning improvements for text-based coding and math, but remains confined to unimodal (text) reasoning. Real-world reasoning increasingly requires grounding in visual information—charts, diagrams, geometric figures—yet extending self-play to multimodal settings is non-trivial since visual tasks lack a natural programmatic verifier analogous to code execution. Proposed Method: We introduce Absolute Zero Multimodal Reasoner (AZ-MM), which extends the AZR paradigm to vision-language models by leveraging a hybrid verification environment: (1) a code executor that programmatically generates synthetic visual reasoning tasks (e.g., matplotlib-rendered charts, geometry diagrams via SVG/PIL, grid-based spatial puzzles) and simultaneously holds ground-truth answers, enabling automatic verification; (2) a self-proposing mechanism where the model proposes visual question generation programs, executes them to produce image-question-answer triples, and then solves the generated visual questions—receiving verifiable rewards without any human-curated data. The model iteratively refines both its task-proposal distribution and its visual reasoning capability through reinforcement learning. Experiments: We evaluate AZ-MM on standard multimodal benchmarks (MathVista, ChartQA, GeoQA, MMStar) against zero-data baselines and supervised RLVR models, ablating task-type curricula, visual complexity schedules, and model scale (3B–72B).

title: Absolute Zero for Scientific Discovery: Self-Evolving Hypothesis Generation and Verification in Structured Scientific Domains
description: Problem: While AZR demonstrates self-play reasoning for code and math, scientific reasoning requires generating and testing hypotheses grounded in domain-specific formal systems (chemistry, physics, biology). Current RLVR approaches lack mechanisms for self-proposing scientifically valid tasks with automated verification beyond code execution. Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to scientific domains by replacing the code executor with domain-specific verifiable environments: a chemistry reaction simulator (RDKit), a physics equation solver (SymPy + numerical integrators), and a formal biology pathway validator. The model simultaneously learns to propose testable scientific hypotheses (as structured queries), solve them, and receive binary verifiable rewards from simulators. We introduce a 'scientific plausibility filter' using constraint satisfaction to ensure proposed tasks lie within physically meaningful parameter spaces, preventing degenerate self-play. A curriculum difficulty estimator tracks task complexity across domains to balance exploration. Experiments: (1) Benchmark against supervised models on chemistry reaction prediction (USPTO-MIT), physics problem-solving (SciBench), and pathway inference tasks. (2) Ablate the plausibility filter's effect on task diversity and learning efficiency. (3) Evaluate cross-domain transfer: does self-play in chemistry improve physics reasoning? (4) Human expert evaluation of novel hypothesis quality generated during training, assessing scientific interestingness beyond benchmark accuracy.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Evolving Task Curricula for Grounded Physical Reasoning
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates impressive self-play reasoning for code and math, its grounded verification relies solely on code executors. Embodied AI agents require physical-world reasoning (spatial, causal, mechanical) that code execution cannot easily verify. Existing embodied RL approaches depend on hand-crafted reward functions and human-designed task suites that limit scalability.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., MuJoCo/PyBullet) as the unified verifiable reward source. A single vision-language-action model simultaneously proposes physical reasoning tasks (e.g., 'predict trajectory of object X given force Y', 'determine minimum force to topple structure Z') and attempts to solve them, using simulator ground truth as verification. The model learns a task proposer that generates tasks at its learning frontier—neither trivially solvable nor impossible—via a learnability signal derived from rolling solve-rate statistics. We introduce Sim-Grounded Chain-of-Thought, where reasoning traces are anchored to physically verifiable intermediate states.

Experiments: (1) Compare against human-curated embodied reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys, RoboSuite); (2) Ablate task proposal strategies (random, curriculum-driven, learnability-maximizing); (3) Test transfer to real-world robot manipulation tasks; (4) Evaluate emergence of physical intuitions (conservation laws, contact dynamics) without explicit supervision.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can bootstrap reasoning through self-generated code tasks with verifiable rewards, but this remains confined to symbolic/mathematical domains. Embodied and physical reasoning—crucial for robotics and scientific modeling—requires grounding in spatial, causal, and temporal relationships that code execution alone cannot verify. Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero framework to embodied reasoning by coupling a language model with a physics simulator (e.g., MuJoCo or Isaac Gym) as the verifiable reward oracle. The model learns to propose tasks across three modes: (1) prediction tasks (forecast trajectory outcomes), (2) inverse tasks (infer initial conditions from final states), and (3) intervention tasks (generate action sequences achieving target configurations). Task difficulty is adaptively controlled via a learnability signal measuring current success rate. A unified reward signal comes from simulator ground truth, requiring no human labeling. Experiments: We evaluate on held-out benchmarks including physical reasoning QA (PHYRE, IntPhys), robotic planning tasks, and novel simulator-generated test sets. We compare against supervised baselines, standard RLVR with human-curated physical reasoning datasets, and ablations removing each task mode. We analyze whether self-generated physical curricula transfer to real-world robotic control tasks via sim-to-real evaluation.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:
Problem: Current self-play RLVR approaches like Absolute Zero succeed in formal domains (code, math) with clean verifiers, but physical/embodied reasoning—crucial for robotics and scientific discovery—lacks analogous self-generating curricula with grounded verification. Human-curated embodied tasks are extremely scarce and domain-limited.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., MuJoCo/PyBullet) as the unified verifiable reward source. A single multimodal LLM acts as both task proposer and solver: the proposer generates parameterized physical scenarios (object configurations, force constraints, causal queries) that are auto-validated for physical feasibility by the simulator, while the solver predicts outcomes verified against simulation rollouts. We introduce a 'physical learnability' score combining task novelty, solver uncertainty, and simulation success rate to guide curriculum progression, analogous to AZR's deduction/abduction/induction task taxonomy but adapted for causal physical reasoning.

Experiments: (1) Zero-data training on physical reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys, virtual robotics manipulation); (2) Ablations comparing task proposal diversity vs. random parameter sampling; (3) Cross-domain transfer: does embodied self-play improve mathematical/causal reasoning on existing benchmarks?; (4) Scaling analysis across model sizes. We hypothesize self-generated physical curricula yield emergent intuitive physics understanding without any labeled examples.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Proposed Interaction Tasks for Grounded Reasoning Without Human Curricula
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates self-evolving reasoning in code/math domains using a code executor as a verifiable reward oracle. However, embodied and tool-using agents operating in interactive environments (web browsers, robotics simulators, API ecosystems) still depend heavily on human-curated task demonstrations. Extending self-play curriculum generation to grounded, multi-step interactive settings remains unexplored.

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, where a single agent model simultaneously (1) proposes executable interaction tasks of varying difficulty within a sandbox environment (e.g., MiniWoB++ browser tasks, simulated file systems, or API sandboxes), (2) attempts to solve them, and (3) receives verifiable binary rewards from environment success signals. A task-proposer head generates structured task specifications; a difficulty controller biases proposals toward the agent's current competence boundary using a windowed success-rate estimator, mirroring AZR's deductive/abductive/inductive trichotomy adapted for sequential decision-making.

Experiments: (1) Curriculum analysis—measure how proposed task complexity evolves over training without human data; (2) Zero-shot transfer to held-out WebArena and ALFWorld benchmarks; (3) Ablations on task-proposal diversity vs. difficulty targeting; (4) Scaling study across 3B/7B/14B models; (5) Comparison against human-curated imitation learning baselines, measuring sample efficiency and generalization gap.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Task Generation in Grounded Simulation Environments
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates self-evolving reasoning curricula for code and math, but remains confined to symbolic domains. Task proposals are filtered for learnability using a difficulty estimator based on current solve rate, mirroring AZR's curriculum mechanism. The simulator provides binary success/failure rewards without human labeling. We train with a joint RL objective over proposer and solver heads sharing a backbone. Experiments: We evaluate on held-out embodied reasoning benchmarks (EmbodiedQA, ALFRED, SQA3D), comparing against supervised baselines and human-curated RL fine-tuning. Ablations examine task diversity, curriculum progression, and transfer to real-robot perception tasks via sim-to-real evaluation.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Curricula via Executable Visual Verification
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can self-generate training curricula without external data using code execution as a verifiable reward oracle. However, this approach is limited to text-based reasoning domains. Vision-language models (VLMs) still depend heavily on human-curated image-question-answer datasets for reasoning improvements, and no analogous self-play framework exists for multimodal reasoning.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to multimodal settings by introducing a self-play framework where a single VLM proposes, solves, and verifies visual reasoning tasks. The model generates synthetic visual reasoning tasks by (1) programmatically constructing verifiable visual scenes using rendering libraries (matplotlib, PIL, SVG generators) that produce images with deterministic ground-truth answers, (2) proposing questions about spatial relationships, geometric properties, chart data, and visual arithmetic, and (3) using the rendering code as an executable oracle to verify answers. The model simultaneously trains its task-proposal and task-solving capabilities through RLVR, with curriculum difficulty adapting based on solve rates.

Experiments: We train on LLaVA/InternVL backbones under zero external data conditions and evaluate on MathVista, GeoQA, ChartQA, and MMStar benchmarks. Ablations examine scene complexity progression, task-type diversity, and cross-domain transfer to real-image benchmarks despite training exclusively on synthetic visual inputs.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description: Problem: Absolute Zero demonstrated that LLMs can bootstrap reasoning through self-generated code tasks verified by a code executor. However, this paradigm is restricted to symbolic/discrete domains (code, math). The self-play curriculum adapts difficulty by modulating object counts, mass distributions, and force configurations based on learning progress signals. We introduce a task proposal module constrained to generate physically coherent scenarios via structured JSON schemas, preventing degenerate proposals. Experiments: We evaluate on held-out physical reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys, ShapeStacks), compare against supervised baselines and standard RLVR with human-curated physical QA datasets, and analyze emergent curriculum structure. We also test cross-domain transfer: does physical reasoning training improve mathematical/logical reasoning?

title: Absolute Zero for Structured Scientific Discovery: Self-Play Curriculum Learning in Chemistry and Biology Reasoning
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero Reasoner (AZR) demonstrates powerful self-evolving reasoning for code and math, its paradigm has not been applied to structured scientific domains like chemistry and biology, where reasoning requires domain-specific grounding (molecular structures, reaction rules, biological pathways) rather than general computation. Extending self-play to these domains is non-trivial because verification requires domain simulators rather than code executors.

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Sci, which replaces the code executor with domain-specific verifiable oracles: (1) RDKit/reaction simulators for chemistry tasks (predict reaction products, retrosynthesis, property prediction), and (2) constraint-based biological network simulators for pathway reasoning. The model self-proposes tasks at three reasoning types (deductive, abductive, inductive) adapted for molecular domains, where task validity and answer correctness are verified programmatically by these simulators. A task difficulty curriculum emerges naturally from molecular complexity metrics (atom count, reaction steps, pathway depth).

Experiments: We benchmark AZR-Sci against supervised baselines on USPTO reaction prediction, ChEBI property reasoning, and KEGG pathway inference. We ablate oracle types and reasoning task distributions. We measure whether self-proposed tasks cluster around chemically meaningful difficulty frontiers and evaluate transfer to held-out scientific benchmarks (MoleculeNet, SciQ-Chemistry), demonstrating cross-domain generalization of the self-play RLVR paradigm.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates impressive self-evolving reasoning in code and math domains with discrete verifiable rewards, extending this paradigm to embodied physical reasoning (e.g., spatial reasoning, causal physical prediction, robotic planning) remains unexplored. Physical environments offer naturally verifiable rewards through simulation, yet generating a self-improving curriculum in continuous, high-dimensional spaces poses unique challenges absent in symbolic domains.

Method: We propose Embodied Absolute Zero (EAZ), where a single model serves dual roles as both task proposer and solver within a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo). The task proposer generates parameterized physical scenarios (object configurations, goal states, constraint specifications) described in structured language, while the simulator acts as the verifiable oracle—replacing the code executor. We introduce a learnability-driven curriculum that estimates task difficulty via success-rate statistics and proposes tasks at the frontier of current capability. A contrastive task filtering mechanism rejects physically implausible or trivially unsolvable scenarios before training.

Experiments: (1) Physical reasoning benchmarks: PHYRE, IntPhys, and custom robotic manipulation tasks; (2) Ablation comparing fixed vs. self-generated curricula; (3) Zero-shot transfer to real-robot instruction following; (4) Scaling analysis across model sizes (1B–13B); (5) Comparison against human-curated embodied reasoning datasets.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Task Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:

The simulator serves as the unified verifiable reward oracle—proposed tasks are validated for physical feasibility, and solutions are verified against simulator ground truth. Task difficulty is regulated via a learnability signal (proposal accepted only if current solver success rate falls in [0.2, 0.8]). The model learns physical intuitions through curriculum self-evolution without any human task demonstrations.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark against human-curated datasets on physical reasoning tasks (PHYRE, IntPhys); (2) Ablate proposer-solver coupling vs. separate models; (3) Evaluate transfer to real robot manipulation zero-shot; (4) Analyze emergent task curriculum complexity over training; (5) Compare simulator-as-verifier vs. learned reward models for physical domains.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Evolving Curricula for Robotic Planning via Simulation-Verified Rewards
description: Problem: Current RLVR approaches for robotic task planning rely on human-curated instruction datasets or expensive real-world demonstrations. Extending the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied domains could enable robots to self-generate increasingly complex planning challenges without human supervision, but verifiable rewards in physical environments are non-trivial to obtain automatically. Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, which adapts the Absolute Zero framework to robotic manipulation and navigation. A single policy-proposer network generates parameterized task descriptions (object configurations, goal states, constraints) in a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet/MuJoCo). The simulator acts as the unified verifier: proposed tasks are validated for physical feasibility (reachability, collision-free initialization), and attempted solutions receive binary success rewards from goal-state detection. The model self-proposes tasks at the frontier of its current capability using a difficulty-calibration mechanism tracking recent success rates per task category. We additionally introduce a 'novelty bonus' rewarding structural diversity in proposed scenarios to prevent curriculum collapse. Experiments: We evaluate on established benchmarks (RLBench, Meta-World, MiniGrid) without any human demonstrations, comparing against BC baselines, RLVR with human curricula, and ablations removing self-proposal or novelty bonuses. We measure sample efficiency, generalization to unseen task configurations, and curriculum diversity metrics across training.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Task Generation in Grounded Simulation Environments
description: Problem: While Absolute Zero Reasoner (AZR) demonstrates impressive self-evolving reasoning through code execution, it remains confined to symbolic domains (math, coding). A task proposer network generates progressively harder simulation scenarios using self-play, guided by a learning progress signal (surprise-based curriculum). The reasoner jointly learns to propose grounded tasks and solve them using chain-of-thought reasoning over physical states. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) held-out physical reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys), (2) zero-shot transfer to robot manipulation planning tasks, (3) ablations comparing simulator vs. code executor as reward oracles, and (4) curriculum difficulty progression analysis. We hypothesize that grounded self-play yields systematic physical intuition beyond what symbolic self-play achieves.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation for Robotic Planning via Simulation-Grounded Rewards
description:

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Evolving Curricula for Robotic Task Planning via Simulation-Grounded Verifiable Rewards
description: Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates self-play RLVR for code and math, embodied AI agents (robots, simulation agents) require multi-step spatial and causal reasoning that cannot be verified by code executors alone. The model self-improves through proximal policy optimization on simulator-verified outcomes, with no human demonstrations. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) zero-shot transfer to standard benchmarks (ALFRED, RLBench, MiniGrid), (2) generalization to novel object combinations unseen during self-play, (3) ablations comparing fixed vs. self-generated curricula, and (4) scaling behavior across model sizes. title: Absolute Zero for Science: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Formal Scientific Reasoning Domains
description:
Problem: While AZR demonstrates impressive self-play reasoning for code and math, scientific reasoning (chemistry, biology, physics) requires integrating domain knowledge with structured inference. Human-curated scientific QA datasets are especially scarce, expensive, and quickly outdated. Can the Absolute Zero paradigm extend to formal scientific domains where correctness can be verified through simulation or established physical laws?

Method: We extend AZR to scientific reasoning by replacing the code executor with domain-specific verifiable oracles: (1) a chemistry reaction simulator (RDKit) for organic chemistry transformations, (2) a physics equation solver for mechanics/thermodynamics problems, and (3) a biological pathway database for metabolic reasoning. The model proposes tasks (reaction prediction, force calculations, pathway queries) at varying difficulty, with oracle feedback providing binary correctness signals. We introduce a 'domain novelty' bonus reward to encourage exploration beyond trivially solvable problems, and a cross-domain transfer mechanism where reasoning patterns from one scientific domain bootstrap another.

Experiments: We evaluate on SciQ, MMLU-Science subsets, ChemBench, and a new held-out physics benchmark. Ablations compare single-domain vs. multi-domain self-play, novelty reward variants, and scaling behavior across 7B/13B/70B models. We analyze emergent task curricula to understand what scientific reasoning strategies the model self-discovers.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Evolving Curriculum Learning in Interactive 3D Environments
description:

A single vision-language-action model proposes spatial reasoning tasks (e.g., 'find the object X given description Y', 'determine if path A is shorter than path B') and solves them, using the simulator's deterministic physics engine as the verifiable reward oracle—analogous to AZR's code executor. The model learns a task-proposal policy that maximizes learning progress via curiosity-weighted rewards, self-generating training curricula spanning increasing spatial complexity. A structured task representation encodes environment state, proposed question, and verifiable ground-truth derivable from simulator state.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark against supervised embodied reasoning baselines on EQA, SpatialBench, and ObjectNav without human-labeled data; (2) Ablate the task-proposal curriculum against random task sampling; (3) Evaluate cross-environment transfer to novel 3D scenes; (4) Scale analysis across model sizes (3B–13B VLA models).

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Evolving Curriculum Learning in Simulated Environments Without Human Task Specification
description:

Three task types mirror AZR's taxonomy: (1) deduction—given a generated geometric figure, derive properties; (2) abduction—identify parameters that produce an observed visual pattern; (3) induction—infer the transformation rule from input-output image pairs. The code executor serves as the unified verifier, confirming both image generation validity and answer correctness without human labels.

Experiments: We train MAZR on LLaVA-style and Qwen-VL base models, evaluating on MathVista, GeoQA, ChartQA, and MMMU. Ablations compare task-type contributions, examine emergent visual chain-of-thought quality, and measure scaling behavior across 3B/7B/13B parameter models.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description: Problem: Current self-play RLVR approaches like Absolute Zero excel at symbolic reasoning (code, math) but cannot generate grounded physical reasoning tasks. Robots and embodied agents need causal, spatial, and temporal reasoning that cannot be verified by code executors alone. Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied domains by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (MuJoCo/PyBullet) as the unified verifiable reward source. The model operates in three modes: (1) Task Proposer—generates natural-language descriptions of physical scenarios with verifiable outcomes (e.g., 'will this stacked configuration topple?'), (2) Program Synthesizer—translates scenarios into simulator-executable scripts, and (3) Reasoner—predicts outcomes before simulation. A curriculum controller selects tasks at the frontier of model competence using uncertainty-based difficulty estimation. The system self-proposes increasingly complex multi-step physical reasoning chains (projectile motion, rigid body dynamics, fluid approximations) without any human-labeled data. Planned Experiments: We evaluate on physical reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys, PTR), compare against zero-setting LLM baselines and supervised approaches, ablate curriculum strategies (random vs. self-proposed), and analyze whether simulator-grounded self-play transfers to real-world physical commonsense QA datasets. We also test cross-domain transfer to mathematical physics word problems.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Evolving Visual-Logical Curriculum Without External Data
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates remarkable success for text-based code and math reasoning, but visual reasoning remains dependent on human-curated image-question-answer datasets. Extending self-play curriculum generation to multimodal settings is non-trivial since image generation and visual verification require new mechanisms beyond code executors. Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Vision, a multimodal extension where the model proposes and solves visual reasoning tasks by programmatically generating verifiable visual environments. Specifically, the model generates Python/SVG/matplotlib programs that render synthetic visual scenes (geometric diagrams, charts, spatial arrangements, logical grids), then proposes questions about these scenes with deterministic answers derivable from the generation program itself. The code executor serves triple duty: rendering the visual, providing ground-truth answers, and validating task well-formedness. We design three task types mirroring AZR's deductive/abductive/inductive trichotomy: (1) scene-to-answer (deductive), (2) answer-to-scene reconstruction (abductive), and (3) visual pattern extrapolation (inductive). Self-play RL with GRPO optimizes both task proposal and answer quality simultaneously. Experiments: We train on LLaVA/Qwen-VL backbones and evaluate on GeoQA, MathVista, CLEVR, and visual analogy benchmarks, comparing against models trained on human-curated visual datasets. We also analyze emergent visual complexity in the self-generated curriculum over training.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation with Visual Code Execution
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can bootstrap reasoning through self-generated tasks verified by code execution, but this approach is fundamentally limited to text/code domains. Extending self-play RLVR to multimodal reasoning (visual mathematics, diagram interpretation, chart analysis) remains an open challenge because visual tasks lack a clean programmatic verifier analogous to code execution.

Proposed Method: We introduce Absolute Zero Vision (AZV), extending the self-play curriculum paradigm to multimodal LLMs. The key insight is using a code executor as a visual oracle: the model generates parameterized visual reasoning tasks (e.g., geometry proofs, function plots, data visualizations) by writing matplotlib/sympy programs that produce images with deterministic ground-truth answers embedded in the generation code. The same model then receives the rendered image and must solve the visual question, with rewards verified against the generative parameters. A difficulty-aware proposer module tracks performance curves per visual category to adaptively sample task complexity, preventing curriculum collapse.

Experiments: (1) Compare AZV against zero-data baselines on MathVista, MMMU, and GeoQA benchmarks; (2) Ablate visual task category distribution (geometry vs. charts vs. plots); (3) Evaluate cross-modal transfer by testing on unseen visual domains; (4) Analyze emergent visual reasoning strategies via attention visualization across training stages; (5) Scale experiments from 7B to 72B parameters.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Evolving Task Curricula for Robot Planning via Simulation-Grounded Verification
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates powerful self-play reasoning for code and math, embodied AI agents—robots that must plan sequences of physical actions—lack analogous data-free training paradigms. Existing robot learning requires expensive human demonstrations or manually designed task suites, creating the same scalability bottleneck AZR addresses for language tasks.

Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied planning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (MuJoCo/IsaacGym) as the unified verifiable reward source. A single vision-language-action model simultaneously (1) proposes manipulation tasks as structured scene configurations and goal predicates, (2) verifies task feasibility via simulation rollouts, and (3) solves proposed tasks using chain-of-thought action planning. Task difficulty is controlled by a curriculum that targets the model's current competency frontier—proposing tasks solvable ~40-60% of the time. Self-play proceeds entirely within simulation without human-labeled demonstrations.

Experiments: We train on Meta-World and RLBench environments, evaluating: (1) zero-shot transfer to unseen held-out tasks versus baselines requiring human demonstrations, (2) curriculum diversity and progression metrics, (3) scaling behavior across model sizes (3B-70B), and (4) sim-to-real transfer on a physical robot arm. We compare against BC-transformer, RT-2, and AZR adapted naively to action spaces.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates self-evolving reasoning for code and math via a code executor as verifier, extending zero-data self-play to embodied physical reasoning (spatial, causal, mechanical) remains unexplored. Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, which replaces the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet/MuJoCo) as the unified verifiable reward source. The single model proposes embodied reasoning tasks (e.g., 'if object A is placed here with force F, where does it end up?') parameterized as simulator configurations, executes them to obtain ground-truth outcomes, then trains itself to predict those outcomes. Task difficulty is self-regulated via a learnability signal: tasks where current model accuracy falls in a target range (30-70%) are prioritized. The model operates in three roles: task proposer (generating simulator-compatible scenario descriptions), reasoner (predicting physical outcomes in natural language), and curriculum manager (selecting tasks maximizing learning progress).

Experiments: Evaluate on PhysicalBench, IntPhys, and CLEVRER benchmarks zero-shot. Compare against supervised baselines and standard RLVR with human-curated physical reasoning datasets. Ablate task proposal diversity, simulator fidelity, and learnability thresholds across model scales (7B-70B).

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation with Visual Code Execution Feedback
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates self-evolving reasoning curricula for text-based coding and math, but multimodal reasoning (combining vision and language) remains dependent on expensive human-annotated image-question pairs. A code executor runs these programs, producing images paired with auto-verifiable ground-truth answers (e.g., 'how many red squares intersect the blue circle?'). The same model then solves its generated visual tasks, receiving verifiable rewards from the executor. The task proposer is trained to maximize learning progress via difficulty-adaptive self-play, mirroring AZR's deduction/abduction/induction task taxonomy but extended to visual modalities. Experiments: We evaluate VAZR on standard multimodal benchmarks (MathVista, GeoQA, ChartQA, MMStar) using no external training data, comparing against supervised multimodal baselines and ablating task type distributions, visual complexity schedules, and model scales (7B–72B). We expect VAZR to demonstrate that programmatic visual synthesis enables scalable multimodal self-improvement.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Evolving Curriculum Learning with Visual Code Execution
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can self-improve through self-proposed tasks verified by code execution, but this approach is limited to text-based reasoning. Multimodal reasoning (combining vision and language) remains heavily dependent on human-curated datasets, and extending self-play to visual domains presents unique challenges since visual inputs cannot be trivially generated or verified by a code executor.

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Vision, which extends the Absolute Zero paradigm to multimodal reasoning by leveraging programmatic generation and verification of visual tasks. The model proposes tasks across three categories: (1) synthetic visual reasoning tasks generated via matplotlib/PIL code (geometric patterns, charts, spatial arrangements), (2) code-grounded visual question answering where images are procedurally generated and answers are verifiable, and (3) visual program synthesis where the model generates code to reproduce described visual outputs. A code executor validates both image generation and answer correctness, maintaining the zero-data paradigm while grounding visual curriculum learning.

Experiments: We train LLaVA/Qwen-VL-scale models using AZR-Vision and evaluate on standard multimodal benchmarks (MathVista, MMStar, MMMU, ChartQA). We compare against supervised multimodal baselines and ablate visual task categories, curriculum difficulty, and model scale. We analyze what visual concepts emerge spontaneously during self-play training.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Evolving Curriculum Learning via Simulation-Grounded Reward in Physical Reasoning Tasks
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates powerful self-play reasoning for code and math, but these domains have clean, deterministic verifiers. Embodied physical reasoning (e.g., robotic manipulation planning, physics-based puzzle solving) lacks such verifiers, yet represents a critical frontier for AI capability. Can a model autonomously generate and solve increasingly complex physical reasoning tasks using a physics simulator as the verifiable reward oracle?

Proposed Method: We extend the AZR framework to physical reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulation engine (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo). The model proposes tasks as structured scene descriptions with goal conditions (e.g., 'stack objects to reach height X given constraints Y'), generates candidate action sequences as solutions, and receives binary rewards from simulator execution. A task-proposer head learns to generate tasks at the frontier of model competence using the same learnability-based reward shaping as AZR, but grounded in simulation outcomes.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate on held-out physical reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys) without training on their data. (2) Ablate task-proposal strategies (random vs. curriculum-driven). (3) Compare against models trained on human-curated physical reasoning datasets. (4) Analyze emergent task complexity curves over training. (5) Test transfer to robotic planning benchmarks (RoboSuite).

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Evolving Curricula for Robot Planning via Simulation-as-Verifier
description:

Can the Absolute Zero paradigm extend to embodied domains where a physics simulator replaces the code executor as the verifiable reward source?

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, a system where a single LLM/VLM simultaneously proposes embodied planning tasks (e.g., object rearrangement goals, manipulation sequences described in natural language) and solves them, using a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or Isaac Gym) as the unified verifier. Task proposals are parameterized as scene configurations and goal predicates; the simulator executes generated robot action plans and returns binary success signals as verifiable rewards. A difficulty-aware curriculum scheduler tracks model competence and steers task proposal toward maximally informative challenges, analogous to AZR's deductive/inductive/abductive task taxonomy but adapted to embodied primitives.

Experiments: (1) Zero-data training on robotic manipulation benchmarks (RLBench, FurnitureBench) vs. IL baselines requiring demonstrations; (2) Curriculum evolution analysis showing task difficulty progression; (3) Cross-embodiment transfer (arm→mobile manipulation); (4) Ablations on task proposal diversity and simulator-in-the-loop verification frequency. Success metric: task completion rate without any human-provided demonstrations.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Evolving Task Curricula in Simulated Physical Environments
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates powerful self-play reasoning for coding and math via code executors as verifiable reward sources. However, embodied reasoning—spatial planning, physics-based problem solving, multi-step manipulation—remains largely dependent on human-curated demonstrations and task specifications. Can an agent self-propose and self-verify embodied reasoning tasks without external data?

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero framework to embodied settings using physics simulators (MuJoCo, PyBullet) as the verifiable reward oracle, analogous to AZR's code executor. A single vision-language-action model simultaneously proposes physically grounded tasks (e.g., 'stack objects satisfying constraint X') and attempts to solve them. Task validity is verified by simulator state checks; solutions are verified by goal-condition satisfaction. We introduce a 'physical plausibility filter' ensuring proposed tasks are neither trivially solvable nor physically impossible, maintaining productive curriculum difficulty. A learnability signal based on recent solve-rate gradients guides task proposal toward the learning frontier.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) zero-shot transfer to standard embodied benchmarks (MetaWorld, RLBench), (2) novel physical reasoning tasks requiring compositional planning, (3) ablations on task proposal strategies, and (4) scaling analysis across model sizes. We compare against imitation learning baselines using equivalent compute budgets, demonstrating that self-generated curricula match or exceed human-curated task suites.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Evolving Curriculum Learning Through Simulated Physical Interaction
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates self-play curriculum learning for code and math reasoning, embodied reasoning tasks (spatial navigation, physical intuition, causal manipulation) remain underexplored in zero-data RLVR frameworks. Physical reasoning requires grounded task generation that respects real-world constraints, making naive task proposal unstable and reward verification non-trivial.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied reasoning by coupling an LLM-based task proposer with a physics simulator (e.g., MuJoCo or PyBullet) as the unified verifiable reward oracle. The model proposes three task types mirroring AZR's trichotomy: (1) Deduction: predict outcome of a described physical scenario, (2) Abduction: infer initial conditions from observed outcomes, (3) Induction: identify physical laws from observation sequences. The simulator executes proposed scenarios and verifies answers, providing binary rewards. A novelty-weighted curriculum ensures tasks remain at the frontier of model capability, filtered by simulator feasibility checks analogous to AZR's code executor validation.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on embodied QA tasks (PHYSICS, PTR, ComPhys) against supervised baselines and standard RLVR. (2) Zero-shot transfer to real robot trajectory planning tasks. (3) Ablations on task-type balance and simulator fidelity. (4) Scaling analysis across 7B-72B model sizes. We hypothesize self-generated physical scenarios bootstrap spatial reasoning beyond human-curated datasets.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation with Visual Code Execution Feedback
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates impressive self-evolving reasoning without external data for text-based tasks, but extending this to multimodal reasoning (combining vision and language) remains unexplored. Human-curated visual QA datasets are even scarcer and more expensive than text datasets, making data-free multimodal reasoning particularly valuable. Proposed Method: We introduce Multimodal Absolute Zero Reasoner (MAZR), extending the AZR framework to vision-language models. The model self-proposes tasks involving matplotlib/PIL-generated synthetic visual inputs (charts, geometric figures, spatial arrangements) paired with code-verifiable questions, using a Python executor as a unified reward signal. The task proposer generates (code_to_render_image, question, solution_code) triples, where the executor both generates the visual stimulus and verifies the answer deterministically. Three task types are proposed: visual deduction (infer properties from rendered plots), visual abduction (identify parameters that produced an observed image), and visual induction (learn patterns across multiple generated images). Experiments: We fine-tune LLaVA-1.6 and InternVL2 variants using MAZR, evaluating on MathVista, GeoQA, ChartQA, and MMStar benchmarks. We ablate the contribution of each visual task type and compare against supervised multimodal baselines and zero-data text-only baselines, demonstrating that self-generated visual curricula improve multimodal reasoning without any human-labeled data.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Evolving Spatial and Physical Task Curricula via Simulation Feedback
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates self-play RLVR for code and math reasoning using a code executor as verifier, embodied and physical reasoning (spatial navigation, object manipulation, physics prediction) remains dependent on human-curated datasets and cannot leverage code execution as a reward signal. Current LLMs and VLMs struggle with grounded physical reasoning precisely because such tasks lack scalable automated verification.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied spatial-physical reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., MuJoCo or PyBullet) as the unified verifiable reward source. A single model simultaneously proposes embodied tasks (described in natural language + structured scene specifications), generates solution plans, and receives binary verification from the simulator. Task proposals are parameterized over object configurations, spatial relationships, and physical constraints. We introduce a 'physical grounding score' to measure task difficulty and ensure curriculum progression, analogous to AZR's degenerate-task avoidance mechanisms.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on EmbodiedQA, SpatialBench, and PHYSICS-IQ against supervised baselines; (2) Ablate simulator-as-verifier vs. code-executor fallback; (3) Measure curriculum progression via task complexity statistics over training; (4) Evaluate zero-shot transfer to real-world robotic planning benchmarks (RLBench). We expect self-play simulation feedback to surpass models trained on human-curated embodied datasets.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description: Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates powerful data-free self-improvement for code and math reasoning, extending this paradigm to embodied, physically-grounded reasoning remains unexplored. Physical reasoning (forces, trajectories, causality) requires spatial intuition that code executors cannot naturally verify, and human-curated embodied reasoning datasets are extremely scarce. Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, extending the Absolute Zero paradigm to physical simulation environments (PyBullet/MuJoCo). The model acts as both a task proposer and solver: it generates parameterized physical scenario descriptions (object configurations, force applications, constraint problems), a simulation executor evaluates feasibility and verifies predicted outcomes against ground-truth simulation rollouts, and RL rewards guide curriculum self-evolution. We design three reasoning task types mirroring AZR's deduction/abduction/induction split: predicting final states (deduction), inferring initial conditions from outcomes (abduction), and discovering physical laws from trajectories (induction). The model generates tasks in structured JSON, executed by the simulator as the unified verifiable reward source. Experiments: (1) Compare AZR-Embodied against human-curated physical reasoning benchmarks (PhysicalIQA, PIQA, IntPhys); (2) Ablate task type contributions; (3) Evaluate transfer to robotics planning tasks; (4) Analyze emergent curriculum difficulty progression; (5) Test cross-scale generalization from 7B to 32B models.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Proposed Interaction Tasks via Simulation-Grounded Verifiable Rewards
description: Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can self-improve reasoning through self-proposed tasks verified by code executors, but this remains confined to symbolic domains (math, code). Embodied AI agents—robots, game-playing agents, GUI navigators—face the same data scarcity bottleneck, yet lack a clean analog of code execution as a verifiable reward oracle. Proposed Method: We extend Absolute Zero to embodied settings by coupling a multimodal language model with a lightweight physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo) as the unified verifiable reward source. The model plays three roles: (1) Task Proposer—generates natural-language task descriptions and initial scene configurations as code-specified simulator states; (2) Task Validator—executes proposed tasks to check solvability and difficulty (filtering trivially easy or unsolvable tasks using simulation rollouts); (3) Task Solver—generates action programs solved within the simulator, receiving binary success/failure rewards. Self-play curriculum emerges as the model iteratively proposes tasks at its competence boundary. We train on zero external embodied demonstration data. Experiments: We evaluate on (a) robotic manipulation benchmarks (RLBench, MetaWorld), (b) GUI navigation (MiniWoB++), and (c) a new diagnostic suite measuring curriculum diversity and difficulty progression. Comparisons against BC baselines trained on human demos and standard RLVR with fixed task sets.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulation Environments
description:
Problem: Current self-evolving RLVR approaches like Absolute Zero are limited to code and math reasoning, where a code executor provides verifiable rewards. Extending data-free self-play reasoning to embodied/physical reasoning tasks (spatial, causal, mechanical) is unexplored, yet critical for robotics and physical AI systems.

Proposed Method: We introduce EmbodiedZero, which replaces the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet/MuJoCo) as the unified verifiable reward oracle. A single model simultaneously proposes embodied reasoning challenges (e.g., 'will this stacked configuration topple?', 'which trajectory reaches the goal?') and solves them, with the simulator providing ground-truth verification. We extend the three task-type framework (deduction, abduction, induction) to embodied analogs: predicting simulation outcomes (deduction), inferring initial conditions from observed outcomes (abduction), and discovering physical rules from trajectory observations (induction). The model generates structured scenario specifications parsed into simulator configs, receives binary/scalar rewards from simulation execution.

Experiments: (1) Physical intuition benchmarks (IntPhys, CRAFT, PTR); (2) Downstream robotics planning tasks; (3) Ablations on task-type curriculum balance; (4) Comparison against models trained on human-curated physical reasoning datasets; (5) Scaling analysis across model sizes 1B-14B. We hypothesize self-generated physical curricula outperform static human-curated datasets on out-of-distribution physical scenarios.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation for Physical World Simulation Tasks
description:
Problem: Current self-play RLVR approaches like Absolute Zero excel at abstract symbolic reasoning (code, math) but cannot reason about physical dynamics, spatial relationships, or causal chains in embodied environments—capabilities critical for robotics and embodied AI. The code executor paradigm provides clean verifiability but limits the task space to purely symbolic domains.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to physics simulation environments (MuJoCo, PyBullet) by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator as the verifiable reward oracle. The model proposes tasks in three modes adapted for embodied reasoning: (1) forward prediction tasks ('given this initial state and action sequence, predict the final configuration'), (2) inverse planning tasks ('what action sequence achieves this goal state?'), and (3) causal counterfactual tasks ('which object modification changes the trajectory?'). Task proposals are parameterized as structured JSON describing object configurations, and the simulator deterministically verifies answers, maintaining the zero-data RLVR property. A learnability filter prevents curriculum collapse to trivially easy or impossible configurations.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) PhysicalBench and PTR physical reasoning benchmarks, (2) zero-shot transfer to real robot manipulation planning, (3) ablations comparing simulator vs. code executor as verification oracle, and (4) scaling analysis across 3B/7B/14B model sizes. title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation for Robotic Planning via Simulation-Verified Rewards
description:
Problem: Current RLVR approaches to robotic task planning rely on human-curated task specifications and costly real-world or simulation demonstrations. Extending Absolute Zero's data-free paradigm to embodied domains could enable robots to autonomously develop complex planning capabilities without human task curation.

Proposed Method: We introduce Embodied Zero Reasoner (EZR), which extends the Absolute Zero paradigm to robotic manipulation and navigation planning. A single LLM-based policy learns to (1) propose embodied planning tasks of graduated difficulty (e.g., multi-step manipulation sequences, spatial reasoning challenges), (2) generate candidate solution plans expressed as executable robot action sequences, and (3) receive verifiable rewards from a physics simulator (e.g., Isaac Gym or PyBullet) that validates whether proposed tasks are physically feasible and whether solution plans achieve success criteria. The model self-regulates curriculum difficulty by tracking success rates and proposing tasks at the frontier of its current capability. We introduce a task validity discriminator that filters physically impossible proposed tasks before simulation evaluation.

Experiments: We evaluate EZR on FurnitureBench, RLBench, and AI2-THOR against baselines using human-curated task datasets. Metrics include task success rate, curriculum progression curves, generalization to held-out task categories, and sample efficiency compared to supervised approaches. We ablate the role of difficulty adaptation and physical validity filtering.

title: Absolute Zero for Structured Scientific Discovery: Self-Evolving Hypothesis Generation and Verification in Formal Domains
description: Problem: While Absolute Zero Reasoner demonstrates self-play curriculum learning for coding and math, the paradigm has not been explored for scientific reasoning domains like chemistry, physics, or biology, where hypotheses can be formally verified against simulation environments or symbolic solvers—potentially enabling autonomous scientific discovery without human-curated data. Proposed Method: We extend the AZR paradigm to structured scientific domains by coupling a language model with domain-specific verifiable environments: molecular property simulators (RDKit for chemistry), physics ODE solvers, and formal logic systems. The model proposes tasks across three modes adapted from AZR—'predict' (given molecule structure, predict property), 'design' (propose structure with target property), and 'explain' (generate mechanistic reasoning chains verified by symbolic solvers). A curriculum controller prioritizes tasks at the boundary of current competence using learning progress signals from verification outcomes. We introduce domain-specific task validity constraints to prevent degenerate proposals. Experiments: We evaluate on held-out benchmarks including ChemBench, GPQA (chemistry/physics subsets), and custom molecular design challenges. Ablations examine: (1) cross-domain transfer from self-generated curricula, (2) emergent discovery of non-obvious chemical rules, (3) scaling behavior across 7B–70B models, comparing against supervised baselines using thousands of human-curated scientific QA pairs.

title: Absolute Zero for Structured Scientific Discovery: Self-Evolving Hypothesis Generation and Verification in Formal Domains
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero Reasoner (AZR) demonstrates impressive self-play reasoning for coding and math, it relies on a code executor as its sole verifiable reward signal. Scientific reasoning domains like chemistry, biology, and physics require structured hypothesis-experiment-verification cycles that go beyond code execution. Can the Absolute Zero paradigm extend to scientific discovery by using domain simulators and formal knowledge systems as verifiable oracles?

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Sci, which replaces the code executor with a suite of domain-specific verifiable oracles: (1) molecular property simulators (RDKit, quantum chemistry packages) for chemistry, (2) formal theorem provers (Lean4) for mathematical physics, and (3) constraint satisfaction solvers for systems biology. The model simultaneously proposes scientific hypotheses/tasks and attempts to solve them, receiving reward signals from these simulators. A curriculum difficulty controller tracks task success rates to maintain self-challenge. We add a 'novelty bonus' rewarding tasks that differ from previously solved ones, encouraging systematic exploration of the domain space.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on chemistry reasoning tasks (USPTO reactions, molecular property prediction), (2) physics theorem proving in Lean4, (3) ablation of oracle types and novelty bonuses, (4) qualitative analysis of emergent scientific problem-solving strategies compared to AZR and supervised baselines, (5) cross-domain transfer evaluation.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation for Spatial and Physical Problem Solving
description:

The model generates task parameters, solves them via chain-of-thought, and receives binary rewards from simulation execution.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) held-out physical reasoning benchmarks (PHYRE, IntPhys), (2) spatial reasoning tasks (ShapeWorld, SpatialBench), (3) robot manipulation planning tasks, comparing against supervised baselines and standard AZR. We ablate task-type curriculum mixing and analyze emergent physical intuition quality across training.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:

Physical reasoning—understanding causality, spatial relationships, and mechanical interactions—requires grounding in continuous environments beyond what a code executor provides. Current embodied AI systems rely heavily on human-designed task curricula and reward specifications.

title: Absolute Zero for Multimodal Reasoning: Self-Evolving Curricula with Visual Code Execution Feedback
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can self-generate training tasks without human data, but this approach is confined to text-only reasoning. Vision-language models (VLMs) still depend heavily on human-curated image-question-answer triplets for reasoning fine-tuning, creating a bottleneck as multimodal tasks grow in complexity.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to multimodal reasoning by enabling a VLM to self-propose visual reasoning tasks grounded in programmatically generated images. Specifically, the model uses a code executor (matplotlib, numpy, networkx) to generate diagrams, geometric figures, charts, and visual puzzles, then formulates questions about these visuals and attempts to solve them. The code executor serves as the unified verifiable reward source: it validates generated visuals are well-formed, and verifies answers by re-executing the generative code with modified parameters. Three task modes are adapted: deduction (given visual, answer question), abduction (given visual and answer, identify generating parameters), and induction (given visual sequence, predict next state). A curriculum difficulty controller modulates complexity of generated visuals based on rolling accuracy.

Experiments: We train Qwen2.5-VL variants using this self-evolving multimodal curriculum and evaluate on MathVista, GeoQA, ChartQA, and MMStar, comparing against zero-setting baselines and human-data-dependent methods. We ablate task type contributions and curriculum scheduling strategies.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:
Problem: Current self-play RLVR paradigms like Absolute Zero excel at symbolic reasoning (code, math) but cannot acquire grounded physical intuition—understanding of causality, spatial relationships, and object interactions—because they lack a physical verification oracle analogous to a code executor. This limits applicability to embodied AI and robotics planning tasks.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to physics-based simulation environments (MuJoCo, PyBullet). The model acts as both a task proposer—generating natural language descriptions of physical scenarios with verifiable outcomes (e.g., 'will object A tip over if placed at angle θ?', 'what is the minimum force to slide block B?')—and a task solver. A physics simulator serves as the unified verifiable reward oracle, replacing the code executor. We introduce a novelty-weighted learnability score that balances task difficulty and simulator-verifiability to drive curriculum progression. The model learns chain-of-thought physical reasoning grounded by simulation feedback, without any human-labeled physics QA data.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on PhysicalQA, PIQA, and ARC physical reasoning subsets; (2) Transfer to robotic manipulation planning (RLBench); (3) Ablations on curriculum difficulty scheduling vs. random task sampling; (4) Scaling analysis across model sizes (3B–32B); (5) Comparison against supervised baselines using human-curated physics datasets.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Grounded Physical Simulation Environments
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero demonstrates powerful self-evolving reasoning via code execution, it remains confined to abstract symbolic domains (math/code). Embodied reasoning—spatial, causal, and physical problem-solving—requires grounding in physical world dynamics, yet suffers from the same data scarcity issues that motivated Absolute Zero. Extending self-play curriculum generation to embodied domains could unlock scalable training for physical reasoning without human-curated task libraries.

Proposed Method: We introduce AZR-Embodied, where a single LLM/VLM simultaneously proposes and solves embodied reasoning tasks grounded in a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo via Python API). The model generates parameterized task descriptions (object configurations, physical queries, causal intervention questions), executes them in simulation to obtain ground-truth answers, and receives verifiable rewards. A task proposer module maintains Goldilocks difficulty via adaptive filtering based on recent solve rates. Three task types mirror AZR's taxonomy: deduction (predict outcome given setup), abduction (infer configuration from observed outcome), and induction (discover physical rules from examples).

Experiments: (1) Physical reasoning benchmarks: PHYRE, IntPhys, PTR; (2) Spatial reasoning: SpatialBench, VSR; (3) Causal reasoning: CRAFT; (4) Ablations on task-type mixture and simulator diversity; (5) Cross-domain transfer to robotics manipulation planning tasks, comparing against human-curated baselines.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Worlds
description:
Problem: While Absolute Zero Reasoner (AZR) demonstrates powerful self-evolving curricula for code and math reasoning, its reliance on a code executor as the verification oracle limits it to symbolic domains. Physical and spatial reasoning—crucial for robotics and embodied AI—requires grounding in continuous, physics-governed environments where self-generated tasks and verifiable rewards are harder to define.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied spatial reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet/MuJoCo) as the unified verifiable reward oracle. A single model jointly proposes parameterized physical tasks (object arrangement puzzles, force/trajectory prediction challenges, multi-step manipulation queries) expressible as simulator configurations, attempts to solve them via chain-of-thought reasoning about physical outcomes, and receives binary verification from simulator execution. Task proposal difficulty is regulated via an adaptive curriculum that tracks model success rates, mirroring AZR's deduction/abduction/induction trichotomy but recast for physical causality.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate spatial/physical reasoning on benchmarks: PHYRE, IntPhys, SpatialBench, and a new self-play-generated held-out test suite. (2) Compare against supervised baselines and AZR adapted with physical QA datasets. (3) Ablate task-type balance (prediction vs. counterfactual vs. planning). (4) Test transfer to robotic manipulation instruction following (RLBench). (5) Analyze emergent task difficulty progression and reasoning chain quality.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Task Generation with Simulated Physical Verification
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can bootstrap reasoning through self-generated tasks verified by code executors, but this approach is inherently limited to symbolic/formal domains. Physical and embodied reasoning—understanding causality, spatial relationships, and object dynamics—remains outside this self-play loop because no verifiable grounding exists for such tasks.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero framework to embodied reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo) as the unified verifiable reward source. A single model learns to propose embodied reasoning tasks (e.g., 'Will stacking these objects cause collapse?', 'What trajectory achieves this goal state?') expressed as simulator-executable scene configurations, then generates natural language reasoning chains and predicted outcomes. The simulator validates proposed tasks for physical feasibility and verifies predicted outcomes, providing binary verifiable rewards. The curriculum self-evolves by tracking prediction accuracy across task difficulty dimensions (object count, interaction complexity, temporal horizon).

Experiments: (1) Evaluate on PhysicalBench, IntPhys, and PHYSICS benchmarks for physical intuition; (2) Compare against supervised baselines and standard RLVR with human-curated physical QA datasets; (3) Ablate simulator types and task proposal strategies; (4) Analyze emergent task curricula and whether models discover physically meaningful difficulty progressions without supervision.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Agents: Self-Proposed Spatial Reasoning Tasks via Simulator-Grounded Reward
description:
Problem: The Absolute Zero paradigm demonstrates that LLMs can self-generate and solve reasoning tasks without human data using code executors as verifiers. However, this remains confined to symbolic/textual domains (code, math). Embodied spatial reasoning—critical for robotics and navigation—requires grounding in physical simulation, where task proposal and verification present distinct challenges.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied spatial reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or Isaac Gym) as the unified verifiable reward source. A single vision-language-action model serves dual roles: (1) a Task Proposer that generates parameterized spatial tasks (object rearrangement, navigation routes, manipulation sequences) with varying difficulty levels, and (2) a Task Solver that executes proposed tasks in simulation. The simulator deterministically verifies success, providing reward signals. We introduce a spatial curriculum difficulty estimator based on geometric complexity metrics (object count, degrees-of-freedom, occlusion level) to ensure tasks remain at the frontier of the model's capability, mirroring AZR's deductive/abductive/inductive task taxonomy but adapted for spatial reasoning modes.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) held-out embodied benchmarks (ScanQA, EmbodiedScan, RoboVQA), (2) zero-shot transfer to real-robot manipulation, (3) ablations on task proposal diversity vs. curriculum progression, and (4) scaling behavior across model sizes from 3B to 32B parameters, comparing against supervised imitation learning baselines.

title: Absolute Zero for Structured Scientific Discovery: Self-Play Curriculum Learning in Symbolic Mathematics and Physical Law Identification
description:
Problem: While AZR demonstrates self-evolving reasoning for coding/math tasks, its task proposal mechanism is tightly coupled to code execution feedback. Scientific discovery tasks—symbolic regression, equation discovery, physical law identification—require generating hypotheses over structured symbolic spaces with richer verification signals beyond pass/fail. Extending self-play RLVR to these domains could enable AI systems that autonomously discover scientific relationships without human-curated datasets.

Proposed Method: We introduce SciZero, a self-play RLVR framework where a single model simultaneously acts as (1) a task proposer generating symbolic regression challenges (e.g., generating synthetic datasets governed by unknown equations) and (2) a solver predicting governing equations. Verification uses symbolic equivalence checking and numerical fitness metrics as grounded reward signals. We augment the task proposal mechanism with a novelty-complexity curriculum that tracks the Pareto frontier of equation complexity vs. discovery difficulty, encouraging exploration of increasingly sophisticated physical relationships.

Experiments: (1) Evaluate on Feynman Symbolic Regression Benchmark without any pre-training on its equations; (2) Compare against supervised baselines on physics equation recovery; (3) Ablate curriculum novelty mechanisms; (4) Test transfer to chemistry kinetics datasets; (5) Analyze emergent symbolic patterns in self-proposed tasks across training. We expect SciZero to discover non-trivial equations matching or exceeding supervised models trained on human-curated datasets.

title: Absolute Zero for Embodied Reasoning: Self-Play Curriculum Generation in Simulated Physical Environments
description:
Problem: Current self-play RLVR approaches like Absolute Zero excel at formal reasoning (code/math) where a code executor provides clean verification, but physical and spatial reasoning tasks—crucial for robotics and embodied AI—lack an analogous grounding mechanism. Human-curated embodied reasoning datasets are extremely scarce and expensive to produce.

Proposed Method: We extend the Absolute Zero paradigm to embodied spatial reasoning by replacing the code executor with a physics simulator (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo) as the verifiable reward oracle. A single model acts as both a task proposer (generating parameterized physical scenarios: object arrangements, force/trajectory questions, causal intervention tasks) and a solver. The simulator validates physical feasibility of proposed tasks and verifies predicted outcomes (e.g., 'will object A fall if B is removed?'). We introduce a dual-difficulty curriculum controller that jointly tracks task proposability rate and solver accuracy to maintain productive learning signal. Tasks span three categories: static stability prediction, trajectory forecasting, and multi-step causal physical reasoning.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on existing spatial reasoning datasets (ShapeStacks, PHYRE, IntPhys) comparing against supervised baselines and zero-setting RLVR; (2) Ablations on simulator-as-verifier vs. model-as-verifier; (3) Scaling analysis across 3B/7B/14B models; (4) Transfer to real-world robotics QA benchmarks. We hypothesize simulator grounding enables robust physical intuition without any human demonstrations.
